name: Sujimori / morigami teased hair

lead: Sujimori (assorted streaks) and morigami (piled-up hair) refer to a styling approach from Japanese gyaru fashion in which hair is built up with volume. The name sujimori comes from the streaks of hair that are held in place with gel, not only from the height of the style. It is seen especially in hime (princess) gyaru looks, which use bleached hair crimped into a bouffant on top, often with curled wigs or extensions.
The visual payoff is a bigger crown, a more dramatic frame around the face and a stylised, glamorous silhouette. The technique is taught in gyaru magazines and salons, and takes practice to do well.

paras: In general terms, hair is lightened or dyed, curled or straightened, teased for volume and sectioned into streaks that are fixed with gel and spray; extensions and wigs are often added to build the shape. Salon styling is common. In the Reiwa-era gyaru revival, simpler and more wearable hair with less extreme volume has been described.

Bleaching and heavy styling products are general hair-care considerations; the style itself has no medical risks. Extreme volume and heavy extensions are less common in the current revival, according to Wikipedia.

chain: Hair is lightened, teased and sectioned into streaks

angle.text: The technique adds visible height and structure to the hair, building a dramatic outline that suits gyaru fashion. Wigs and extensions can supply volume that natural hair lacks.

lead: Sujimori (スジ盛り, 'assorted streaks') is a hair-styling technique from Japanese gyaru fashion. Its name comes from streaks of hair held in place with gel, not just from the volume, and it is linked to the broader morigami (盛り髪, 'piled-up hair') approach, according to Wikipedia's article on gyaru.[1] It is often executed with extensions or wigs and in salons, and takes practice to do well.[1]

It is most associated with hime gyaru, a rococo-inspired subtype in which hair is bleached, crimped into a bouffant on top and paired with curled wigs or extensions to produce sujimori-style volume.[1] Magazines such as Popteen, egg and Koakuma Ageha were prominent in spreading gyaru styles, with some of them carrying hair and makeup guides.[1]
The look is stylised rather than natural: it makes the head and hairline larger and more sculpted, which is the reason people adopt it as part of a gyaru look.
infobox: Hime gyaru; bouffant with extensions or wigs[1]

paras: Gyaru hair is usually bleached or dyed, curled with an iron or straightened, and often teased for volume.[1] Sujimori sets teased streaks in place with gel; extensions and wigs are often used, and salon styling is common.[1] Hime gyaru adds a crimped bouffant on top.[1] Hime-kaji, a casual variant associated with the brand Liz Lisa, peaked between 2010 and 2013 according to Wikipedia.[1]

Gyaru culture developed from the 1970s onward, and substyles such as kogal (early 1990s) and ganguro (late 1990s to early 2000s, with deep tans and bleached hair) preceded the hime and sujimori looks that peaked around 2010-2013.[1] Print magazines have largely been replaced by Instagram, TikTok and X as sources of styling content.[1]
The Reiwa-era revival (2019 onward) emphasises diversity and individual expression, with simpler hair such as loose waves and ponytails, less extreme volume, and wigs styled to look more natural.[1]
